item.title: DbContext Lifetime Management: Per-Request vs. Transient vs. Factory Patterns
item.description:
“DbContext Lifetime Management: Per-Request vs. Transient vs. Factory Patterns”

Understanding DbContext Lifetime Management

The way a DbContext instance is managed throughout an application’s lifecycle significantly impacts performance, resource utilization, and the correctness of data operations. A single, poorly managed DbContext can lead to stale data, concurrency issues, memory leaks, and unexpected behavior, especially in multi-user or multi-threaded environments.

The Case Against a Single Application-Wide DbContext

A common misconception is that a single DbContext instance for the entire application is a viable approach. This is generally a detrimental practice. DbContext instances cache data, and this cache can quickly become outdated, leading to inconsistencies when multiple users or application instances interact with the same database. The only scenario where this might seem acceptable is in a highly specialized, single-threaded application with exclusive database access, which is rarely the case.

item.title: Entity Framework Many-to-Many with Custom Join Table: Strategies and Solutions
item.description:
“Entity Framework Many-to-Many with Custom Join Table: Strategies and Solutions”

When working with Entity Framework (EF) and requiring a many-to-many relationship, you might encounter the need to store additional information in the join table. EF typically handles the join table internally and abstracts it away in a pure many-to-many setup. However, when you need to add custom properties to this intermediate table, a different approach is necessary. This post delves into various methods and code examples for achieving this, offering practical solutions and insights.

How should one approach the initialization of these distinct navigation property types?

item.title: Entity Framework Querying Composite Keys: Effective Strategies Compared
item.description:
“Entity Framework Querying Composite Keys: Effective Strategies Compared”

Consider a scenario where you need to select entities based on marked pairs of Id1 and Id2:

| Id1 | Id2 | Match | |

Solutions

–|

Id1  Id2
---  ---
1    2 *
1    3
1    6
2    2 *
2    3 *
... (many more)
from entity in db.Table // db is a DbContext
join pair in Tuples on new { entity.Id1, entity.Id2 }
                equals new { Id1 = pair.Item1, Id2 = pair.Item2 }
select entity
from entity in db.Table.AsEnumerable() // fetch db.Table into memory first
join pair Tuples on new { entity.Id1, entity.Id2 }
             equals new { Id1 = pair.Item1, Id2 = pair.Item2 }

where ids1.Contains(entity.Id1) && ids2.Contains(entity.Id2)
select entity
var computed = ids1.Zip(ids2, (i1,i2) => i1 * i2); // [2,6]
from entity in db.Table
where computed.Contains(entity.Id1 * entity.Id2)
select entity
from entity in db.Table
where computed.Contains("Id1=" + entity.Id1 + "," + "Id2=" + entity.Id2)
select entity
var rawSelection = from entity in db.Table
                   where ids1.Contains(entity.Id1) && ids2.Contains(entity.Id2)
                   select entity;

var refined = from entity in rawSelection.AsEnumerable()
              join pair in Tuples on new { entity.Id1, entity.Id2 }
                              equals new { Id1 = pair.Item1, Id2 = pair.Item2 }

item.title: Entity Framework Bulk Insert Performance: Strategies and Solutions
item.description:
“Entity Framework Bulk Insert Performance: Strategies and Solutions”

Performing bulk inserts with Entity Framework can often lead to performance bottlenecks due to the overhead of processing individual records. This question delves into various techniques and alternative approaches to accelerate the insertion of large datasets.

Solution 1: Batching SaveChanges and Context Management

A common performance killer is calling SaveChanges() for each record. Instead, consider these strategies:

  1. Single SaveChanges() Call: Execute SaveChanges() only once after all records have been added to the context.
  2. Batched SaveChanges(): Call SaveChanges() after a fixed number of records (e.g., every 100 records).
  3. Batched SaveChanges() with Context Re-creation: After saving a batch of records, dispose of the current context and create a new one. This clears out tracked entities, preventing context bloat.
  4. Disable Change Detection: Temporarily disabling AutoDetectChangesEnabled can yield substantial speed improvements.
